source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1985; pub. 1986/2010) Rapid Decision Making on the Fire Ground (ARI Tech Report 796)
finding: Founding study. Interviews with fireground commanders about non-routine incidents. The team expected commanders to compare two options. They did not. Commanders mostly saw the situation as typical and acted on the first option that fit.
numbers: 26 officers (6 lieutenants, 4 captains, 16 chiefs), mean 23.2 years of firefighting, range 12 to 37. 29 interviews (about 2 hours each, taped) on 32 incidents (29 fires, 2 rescues, 1 gas leak). 156 decision points, about 5 per incident (range 1 to 10). Incident chosen because it was a command challenge or non-routine.
limits: Retrospective interviews only. Only non-routine incidents. Officers not randomly sampled.
agent_relevance: The base design for 'take the first workable option' comes from interview data on hard cases, not from a controlled test. Our scaffold should treat it as a descriptive claim, not proof the first option is best.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1985; pub. 1986/2010) Rapid Decision Making on the Fire Ground (ARI Tech Report 796)
finding: Strategy counts. About 4 in 5 decision points were handled by recognition of a prototype, with no comparison. Concurrent comparison was rare even in hard cases.
numbers: 127 of 156 decision points (81%) fell in the prototype group (the table is garbled in the scan; text says 127). Deliberated (options consciously contrasted): 10 outside the pumping-station fire, 18 with it. Constructed (new option built): 11 in total. Analog matches: 3. Only 28 of 156 had more than one option even identified. Only 16 showed any relative evaluation. The published abstract says under 12% had simultaneous comparison and over 80% were recognition.
quote: we found virtually no instances of the standard laboratory paradigm for decision making: conscious and deliberate selection of one alternative from several.
limits: The 'decision point' was defined by the coders. Options were often supplied by the interviewers (hypothetical novice options). 80% is a share of coded points, not of all choices made.
agent_relevance: Number to quote is 81% (127/156), not 'always'. Roughly 1 in 5 points still needed a different mode (deliberate or construct). Our agent needs a fallback path for that fifth.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1985; pub. 1986/2010) Rapid Decision Making on the Fire Ground (ARI Tech Report 796)
finding: Time pressure was real. Most points were decided very fast. Deliberated and constructed decisions were the ones with more time.
numbers: Time pressure rating (4-point scale, rated by the researchers): 61% of points at level 3 or 4 (imminent loss of control or threatened life), 36% at level 2, 3% at level 1. Most decisions under one minute; about 10% under 2 minutes and 6% between 2 and 5 minutes (scan text for exact shares is unclear). Table 5: Deliberated and Constructed points were made under less time pressure and took longer than prototype points.
limits: Times were estimated from memory. Short times were all coded as 'under one minute'. Time pressure was largely inferred by the coders.
agent_relevance: Support for the idea that keep-first is a time-saving mode. Ties the choice of mode to time and stakes, which fits our rule that the program, not the model, picks the mode.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1985; pub. 1986/2010) Rapid Decision Making on the Fire Ground (ARI Tech Report 796)
finding: A mismatch, not a match, can also drive action. The cue that something does not fit triggers reassessment. This is the origin of 'expectancy violation' in the model. Prototypes also hold an ordered queue of actions.
numbers: 3 of the 156 points were mismatch events. Case 4: a crew entered a house, water on the apparent fire had no effect, it got hot and quiet, the commander pulled the crew out, and the floor collapsed a minute later (the fire was in the basement). Rescue case: dominant response (Kingsley harness), then immediate backup (Howd strap).
limits: Three cases only. The 'sixth sense' reading is the authors' inference.
agent_relevance: Maps to our G1/G2: keep going on the first option until a check shows a mismatch, then re-diagnose from the actual surprise. The action queue is a ready-made 'next candidate' list.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1985; pub. 1986/2010) Rapid Decision Making on the Fire Ground (ARI Tech Report 796)
finding: Boundary case: a long, unique fire (oil pumping station, counted as 3 incidents) where local crews were not experts. Most decisions there were deliberated, in groups.
numbers: About 59% of pumping-station decision points were consciously deliberated, almost always in group consultation. 22 of the 156 points came from these 3 incidents. The fire took almost a week to contain.
limits: Authors flag it as a different command situation and report it separately. It can be read as 'deliberation is for novices and groups' or as 'deliberation is for slow, unique problems'.
agent_relevance: Tells us when keep-first should not run: no expertise in the situation, unique scale, group decision, long time. A router should check whether the situation is typical for the model before keeping the first answer.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1985; pub. 1986/2010) Rapid Decision Making on the Fire Ground (ARI Tech Report 796)
finding: Method limits written by the authors. Decision points were largely inferred. Officers did not feel they were choosing. Interviewers probed for options a novice might consider. No formal inter-coder reliability.
numbers: Coding took 3 to 7 hours per incident. 7 interviews had only one interviewer. Quality control was informal reading and criticism by a second team member and the two principal investigators.
limits: No inter-rater statistic. Possible hindsight and reconstruction bias in interview accounts.
agent_relevance: When we cite RPD numbers in the schema, mark them [S] (single source, interview data) until independent replications are counted. Do not present 80% as measured real-time behaviour.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1985; pub. 1986/2010) Rapid Decision Making on the Fire Ground (ARI Tech Report 796)
finding: The core claim was a serial, not concurrent, option model. One option is generated, then used or rejected, then the next. Prototype recognition supplies the 'if x then y'. The skill sits in situation assessment.
numbers: Fig. 1a (concurrent: options by dimensions) versus Fig. 1b (serial: generate, implement or reject, next). Authors say the serial model fits the data better. Procedural rules vs prototypes: they could not separate them in practice; a rule is context-free and a prototype is context-rich.
limits: The serial model was inferred from what officers said. It was not tested against a rival model on the same data.
agent_relevance: The clearest statement of generate-test, keep-first: one candidate at a time, test it, move on. The expertise is in what gets generated first, which a language model must get from its own priors.

source: Klein & Calderwood (1990) Investigations of Naturalistic Decision Making and the RPD Model (ARI Research Note 90-59)
finding: Expert vs novice fireground commanders (critical decision method). Most decision points were situation assessment. Only a small share were concurrent comparison. Experts used a mix of serial and concurrent strategies; novices leaned on concurrent deliberation.
numbers: 12 experts (mean 19.5 years firefighting, 11 as officer) vs 12 novices (mean 10 years, under 2 as officer), six midwestern city departments. 54% of decision points were situation-assessment decisions, 14% were implementation or timing of a preferred option, 32% involved evaluating between options, of which 14 points were serial. So only 18% fit classical concurrent comparison. Experts constructed novel options more often, used imagery and weighed options more often than novices, and were almost twice as likely to consider future contingencies.
limits: Small cells (12 each). Report-level source (Calderwood, Crandall, Klein 1987), not a journal paper. Novices were not true beginners (10 years).
agent_relevance: Experts differed in what they deliberated about (the situation), not in whether they thought. The scaffold should put checking effort on the situation reading, not on a list of rival answers.

source: Klein & Calderwood (1990) Investigations of Naturalistic Decision Making and the RPD Model (ARI Research Note 90-59)
finding: Lower expertise still shows recognitional decisions. Tank platoon trainees used limited option deliberation and recognition-primed implementation about equally. Analogues helped only about half the time.
numbers: Armor Officer Basic students at Fort Knox (three classes, interviewed within 20 minutes of exercises) vs track commander instructors. The two methods of resolution were about equal in frequency. Analogues helped about half the time, the rest neutral to disruptive. Trainees reported the same cues as instructors but made fewer 'hypotheticals', especially abstract ones (platoon control, communications, enemy).
limits: Sample sizes not given in the summary I read. Self-rating and instructor rating of performance only.
agent_relevance: Failure was not missing cues but misreading their importance. Same as a language model that sees all facts and weights them wrongly. Analogy (retrieval of a similar case) is a coin flip, so a retrieved example needs a check.

source: Klein & Calderwood (1990) Investigations of Naturalistic Decision Making and the RPD Model (ARI Research Note 90-59)
finding: Analogue use in decisions. Re-read of five critical-decision studies for use of specific past cases. Analogues were rare and worked more as flags than as templates.
numbers: Over 400 decision points from over 100 decision makers in five studies (two urban fire, tank platoon, wildfire, Air Force design engineers). 33 analogues were detailed enough to analyse. Three functions: understand dynamics, generate options, evaluate options.
limits: 33 analogues out of 400+ points is about 8%. The pooled data came from the same research group.
agent_relevance: Recognition in the model is mostly prototype matching, not case retrieval. A scaffold that retrieves past solved cases is a related but different thing.

source: Klein & Calderwood (1990) Investigations of Naturalistic Decision Making and the RPD Model (ARI Research Note 90-59)
finding: First test of 'skilled players rely on recognition' in chess under time pressure. Masters lost less move quality in blitz than weaker players.
numbers: 3 masters vs 3 class B players, double round-robin, 24 games (6 per cell). Regulation (at least 50 moves in 2 hours) vs blitz (6 minutes per player). Moves rated 1 to 5 by a grandmaster. Skill by game-type interaction found: class B dropped more in blitz. Published as Calderwood, Klein, Crandall (1988) Am J Psychol.
limits: Tiny sample. Vidulich and Tsang (2026) point out the rater did not separate the groups in regulation games.
agent_relevance: The inference 'time pressure hurts experts less so they do not deliberate' has not survived stronger tests (see later lines).

source: Klein, Thordsen, Calderwood (1990) Descriptive Models of Military Decision Making (ARI Research Note 90-93)
finding: RPD applied to military planning. Four parts of situation assessment (goals, cues, expectancies, typical action). Seven stated differences from decision analysis. Teams used the same recognitional strategy as individuals.
numbers: Sources: urban fire commanders, wildland incident teams, Army armored division personnel, Army battle planners. Fort Hood simulated battalion exercise: a 5-hour planning session had 27 decision points and only 1 compared options. A wildland fire and a Corps-level command post exercise at Fort Leavenworth were also observed. The team hypothesis (more analysis to help communication) was not supported.
limits: Observation of exercises, not scored experiments. One observed battalion planning session.
agent_relevance: Direct military-planning evidence for single-course-of-action planning. The red-team implication is in the next line.

source: Klein, Thordsen, Calderwood (1990) Descriptive Models of Military Decision Making (ARI Research Note 90-93)
finding: The authors warn where the recognitional strategy fails: the commander lacks experience, cannot simulate the option to find pitfalls, or fails to optimise when needed. Enemy course of action analysis needs worst-case thinking, where recognition can mislead.
numbers: Qualitative statement. Generic analytic-process training (decision analysis, multi-attribute utility, Bayes) 'was not very successful', but the authors do not propose RPD process training as its replacement.
limits: Statement of the founders, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: For red teaming: keep-first mode should be off when the task is to find what an adversary could do. That task needs forced generation of bad cases, the opposite of keep-first.

source: Klein & Crandall (1990) Recognition-Primed Decision Strategies: First-Year Interim Report (ARI Research Note 90-91)
finding: Early statement of RPD as the recognitional end of a decision continuum (after Hammond's cognitive continuum), with analytic methods (multi-attribute utility, decision analysis, elimination by aspects) at the other end. Reports a planned test of situation assessment with Army officers that could not be run.
numbers: Domains named: fireground command, battle planning, critical care nursing, corporate information management, chess tournament play. The planned Command and General Staff College experiment hit 'practical barriers' and moved to MBA students at Wright State (experienced vs fresh) as the expert/novice contrast.
limits: Interim report. The planned military-officer experiment was not done.
agent_relevance: A controlled military test of RPD was planned and dropped. Consistent with the missing controlled evidence in our E12 index.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for Intuitive Expertise: A Failure to Disagree. American Psychologist
finding: Joint account by the main RPD author and the main critic. Origin: the team expected commanders to compare a pair of options; that was wrong; commanders usually generated a single option. The option is checked by mental simulation (progressive deepening, after de Groot), modified if flawed, replaced by the next if it cannot be fixed. They say it was replicated in system design, military command and control, and offshore oil installations.
numbers: Fireground source: Klein et al. 1986. Lab tests named: Johnson & Raab 2003; Klein, Wolf, Militello, Zsambok 1995. NDM crystallised at a 1989 meeting of 30 researchers.
quote: the commanders usually generated only a single option, and that was all they needed.
limits: Narrative review. 'Replicated' here means the same finding in other field domains, not a pre-registered replication.
agent_relevance: The accepted description of the loop: recognise, generate one, simulate, modify or move on. This is the shape of our generate-test, keep-first mode.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for Intuitive Expertise (boundary conditions)
finding: Agreed conditions for trusting the first recognised option: a high-validity environment and enough practice to learn its cues. Without these a first answer comes from heuristics and feels equally sure. There is no inner marker to tell the two apart.
numbers: Examples: long-term political forecasting (Tetlock) is low validity. Shanteau 1992 lists of fields with and without expertise. 'Fractionated expertise': nurses, physicians and auditors are good at some tasks and not others. Bat-and-ball problem: unchecked first answer wrong for about 50% at top US universities and about 90% at less selective ones (Frederick 2005). Chess masters need about 10,000 hours (Chase & Simon 1973).
quote: There is no subjective marker that distinguishes correct intuitions from intuitions that are produced by highly imperfect heuristics.
limits: Kahneman and Klein still differ on how common unskilled intuition is.
agent_relevance: Keep-first only if the model has strong priors in that domain and a check can catch an error. For a language model, 'validity and practice' maps to: the task type is well covered in training and an outside check exists.

source: Kaempf, Klein, Thordsen, Wolf (1996) Decision Making in Complex Naval Command-and-Control Environments. Human Factors
finding: Study of experienced officers in the AEGIS cruiser combat information center. Decisions fit RPD. Most decisions were about situation awareness and diagnosis. Abstract only was read (via Crossref).
numbers: Recognitional strategy identified 95% of actions; multiple options compared in 4% of cases (abstract).
limits: Abstract only. Incidents were recalled critical incidents.
agent_relevance: Strongest military figure: 95% recognition. Detail in the next line from a review that read the full paper.

source: Systematic review: Decision-Making During High-Risk Events (J Cogn Eng Decis Mak 2023;17(2):188-212)
finding: Review of 32 empirical papers (19 in healthcare). RPD strategy was found in all studies that looked at strategy. Analytical strategies appear more when time pressure is lower and when training asks for several explanations. Mental simulation is often skipped.
numbers: Table 3 (10 studies). Naval officers (Kaempf 1996): 95% (74 actions) recognitional, 4% (3 actions) multiple options, 1% (1 action) novel; 78% of recognition-generated actions were implemented with no further evaluation; 87% of situation assessment was feature matching, 12% story building. Surgeons: 50% (6 of 12 cases) one option (Pauley 2013); 46% (11 of 24 cases) one option, 50% (12) compared, 4% (1) procedure (Pauley 2011). Experienced fire commanders went from assessment to execution more often than less experienced. Two studies found self-reported time pressure had no significant effect on strategy.
limits: Strategy coding differs across studies. Most studies did not look for creative strategies. Qualitative synthesis, not a pooled effect size.
agent_relevance: Strongest cross-domain count. RPD is the commonest mode but not near 100%, and in surgery with a pre-plan it is about half. The 'skipped simulation' finding says the check step is the weak link in humans too.

source: Ross, Klein, Thunholm, Schmitt, Baxter (2004) The Recognition-Primed Decision Model. Military Review (Jul-Aug)
finding: Army doctrine proposal. The Recognition Planning Model (Schmitt & Klein) builds one base course of action, tests and wargames it, and drops the compare-three-COAs step of the MDMP. A 2003 Fort Leavenworth battle lab experiment and a Swedish division-level study tested it.
numbers: 2-week BCBL experiment, ad hoc brigade staff, 2 days training, 5 days exercise. Participants estimated the RPM took at least 30% less time than MDMP. Thunholm (Swedish Army division-level planning groups, RPM variant vs Swedish MDMP): planning tempo about 20% faster, plans somewhat bolder and better fitted. The pre-mortem was optional but the staff ran it every rotation and moved it earlier. No sunk-cost resistance when a fragmentary order forced replanning.
limits: Preliminary findings, self-estimated time saving. Authors are the RPM developers. Plan quality was judged, not scored on an outcome measure. Units lacking mission experience make worse plans with either method. Participants tended to rush mission analysis.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to a field test of keep-first planning: positive on time, neutral to positive on quality. It also added a pre-mortem because the first option can be wrong, so a check was added to the keep-first rule.

source: Ross et al. (2004) Military Review (claims about earlier lab work)
finding: The authors cite lab support: skilled players usually generate a good course of action first (Klein, Wolf, Militello, Zsambok 1995); Johnson and Raab (2003) replicated this and found later options were worse; Johnston, Driskell, Salas (1997) found intuitive processes beat analytical ones.
numbers: No sample sizes in this article. Claim: when skilled decision makers abandon the first COA for a later one, the later one's quality is significantly lower.
limits: Second-hand. I could not open Klein 1995 or Johnson & Raab 2003 this session (publisher pages blocked), so exact numbers are not recorded.
agent_relevance: If 'later options are worse' holds for language models, best-of-N from fresh samples may not beat the first valid answer. Untested for LLMs; put it on the experiment list.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications 11:35
finding: Strongest recent test against the intuition-first reading of RPD. Elite chess players made more and bigger blunders under time pressure, and used time strategically (fast when easy, slow when needed).
numbers: Study 1: 20 grandmasters, standard games (about 3 min per move) vs blitz (about 7.5 s per move), within subject. Proportion of blunders t(19)=6.54, d=1.39; blunder size t(19)=4.23, d=0.96 (about half a pawn bigger). Expected blunder per move nearly doubled in blitz: t(19)=-5.79, p<.001, d=1.30; worse for 18 of 20 players. Study 2: 11 world championship matches, 7 champions: blunder rate spiked on fast moves just before the time control (moves 36 to 40).
limits: Chess is a closed, high-validity domain; blunders scored by Fritz 9.0. Archival data. The authors target the 'intuition is the main basis of expertise' reading; Klein's model itself includes deliberate simulation.
agent_relevance: In a closed game with fast feedback, forced speed hurt even the best. Fast keep-first costs accuracy when a better deliberate path exists. Supports G1: switch to checks on a signal, and do not treat speed as free.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) (review section on earlier chess work)
finding: Summary of mixed chess evidence on take-the-first. Several classic pro-intuition results are weak or contested.
numbers: Burns 2004: blitz rank scores explained 64 to 81% of variance in slower-game rank (19 to 36% unexplained). Calderwood et al. 1988: 3 vs 3 players. Gobet & Simon: Kasparov in simultaneous play dropped from Elo 2750 to 2646 (Montero; Van Harreveld: about 60th place). Chabris & Hearst 2003: grandmasters (Elo 2530 to 2790) made more and larger blunders in 15-minute games. Moxley et al. 2012: players chose their first mentioned move as final 45% of the time; 22% and 25% (stronger, weaker) on hard positions, 73% and 50% on easy ones; final moves were better than first moves.
limits: Second-hand summary by authors who argue against the intuition account.
agent_relevance: Take-the-first holds on easy items and fails on hard ones. A scaffold should estimate difficulty cheaply before choosing keep-first, and compare first and later answers on held-out checks.

source: Kopka (2026) Increasing LLM Accuracy for Care-Seeking Advice Using Prompts Reflecting Human Reasoning Strategies. JMIR Biomedical Engineering 11:e88053
finding: Only direct LLM test of an RPD prompt found. A recognition-primed prompt (recall a typical case, simulate the usual decision, modify if it fails, otherwise reassess until familiar) raised accuracy on triage advice versus a plain prompt. A data-frame prompt did similarly.
numbers: 10 ChatGPT models (GPT-4o, 4.1, 4.1 mini, o3, o4 mini, o4 mini high, GPT-5.1 Instant and Thinking, GPT-5.2 Instant and Thinking), 45 real patient vignettes, 10 runs each, 3 prompts = 13,500 assessments. Accuracy: default 63.3% (95% CI 61.9 to 64.7), recognition-primed 67.6% (66.3 to 69), data-frame 66.7% (65.3 to 68). Mixed logistic regression: RPD OR 2.26 (z=8.69, p<.001); data-frame OR 2.05. Gain larger for reasoning models than non-reasoning (OR 2.15 for the RPD prompt).
quote: Does this situation match any typical cases you know? If yes, what is the usual decision for such a case? Simulate implementing this decision
limits: One task (self-triage), 45 vignettes of which only 2 emergency and 30 non-emergency; only OpenAI models in ChatGPT; no human users; no length-matched 'think step by step' control (the paper compares to a plain prompt).
agent_relevance: Small positive evidence for an RPD-style prompt with a simulate-and-modify step like our keep-first mode. Missing: a length-matched reasoning control.

source: Kopka (2026) JMIR Biomed Eng (subgroup and model-level results)
finding: The gain came from one category (self-care advice) and was absent in the newest model family. Non-reasoning models that never advised self-care started doing so under the RPD prompt. GPT-5.2 did not respond.
numbers: Self-care accuracy: 13.4% default to 29.8% recognition-primed (24.6% data-frame). GPT-4.1 self-care 0% to 43.8% (RPD) and 39.2% (data-frame). o4 mini 46.9% to 63.8% (RPD) and 56.2% (data-frame). Largest single-model gain: GPT-4.1 mini +13 points (95% CI 9.7 to 16.1) with data-frame. GPT-5.2 Instant and Thinking: self-care accuracy 0% under all prompts. Emergency cases: 100% default, 99% and 98% with the prompts.
limits: Ceiling effects on emergency and non-emergency cases. 88% of all errors were over-triage. Results held at low temperature (appendix tables). The GPT-5.2 failure is not explained.
agent_relevance: The prompt corrected a bias (over-cautious advice); it did not add skill. The effect may vanish when a model update already removes the bias. Do not count on prompt-level RPD for gains.

source: Kopka (2026) JMIR Biomed Eng (case-level, consistency and cost)
finding: Mixed effect at case level, and a cost. The RPD prompt hurt some cases, did not make answers more stable, and adds output tokens.
numbers: RPD prompt raised accuracy in 18 of 45 cases (40%) and lowered it in 13 (29%); median rise 18% (IQR 5 to 24), median fall 5% (IQR 2 to 7). 12 of 13 decreases were non-emergency cases. Same-answer reliability (Fleiss kappa, median): default 0.766, RPD 0.717, data-frame 0.751. Most frequent answer share: 76.9%, 66.9%, 71.1% (no significant difference). Correct at least once in 10 runs: 73.1% default vs 82.2% RPD vs 78.4% data-frame.
limits: No matched-length control and no test on well-defined tasks. Authors say benefits are 'thus far limited to uncertain tasks'.
agent_relevance: A pass-at-10 gain (73.1 to 82.2) with a modest majority-answer gain means the prompt widens what the model can say more than it fixes the default. Select with an outside check, not by trusting the first answer (G5).

source: Heander, Soderberg, Rydenfalt (2025) Code Review as Decision-Making. arXiv 2507.09637
finding: Software-engineering use of RPD. A think-aloud study of code review is mapped onto the RPD model: an orientation phase (the preparatory half of the model) and an analytical phase (one full RPD cycle: expectancies, cues, action, mental simulation).
numbers: 10 developers, 34 code reviews, mean 19 min (SD 18; range 1 to 75), 1159 process-coded segments; 26 of 34 reviews got a vote of at least +1. Most experienced participant had 17 years of code review. The model is said to explain why even experienced programmers can need up to a year in a new workplace to become effective reviewers (cites Bosu 2015).
limits: Qualitative, one Swedish company, volunteers; not an LLM study and not a test of RPD against a rival. The mapping is the authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Code review by an LLM agent could follow the same two phases: build expectations from the change rationale, then check the code against them and simulate. A design hint, not evidence of benefit.

source: Bossard, Krerival, Dugeny, Bagot, Fontaine, Kermarrec (2022) Naturalistic decision-making in sport (RPD). Frontiers in Psychology 13:936140
finding: Sport review of RPD: the three levels and the shares seen in sport studies. Intuitive simple match dominates, but time available shifts the mix. Handball goalkeepers and soccer defenders far from the ball had more time to simulate; rugby coaches under less pressure used more deliberate decisions.
numbers: Macquet (2020) review cited: 60 to 81% of expert decisions simple match, 13 to 28% diagnosis, 3 to 24% evaluating a course of action. Expert athletes chose their preferred first option in about 80% of decisions (sport studies cited).
limits: Second-hand figures from a review I did not open. Mostly qualitative interview studies with retrospective accounts.
agent_relevance: The share of recognition vs deliberation moves with time available: a scaffold can use available time as an input to the mode choice.

source: Ashford, Abraham, Poolton (2021) Understanding a Player's Decision-Making Process in Team Sports: Systematic Review. Sports 9(5):65
finding: 53 articles; four studies tested RPD in team sports and all fit the level model: familiar situations give a simple match (level 1), atypical ones evoke explicit diagnosis (level 2), mental rehearsal of multiple courses is level 3. Whether a mental representation is used depends on complexity, typicality, time available and context.
numbers: 53 included articles from 9 databases searched to March 2021. Four studies on RPD in team sports. One included study had Brazilian players generate more options and also be more accurate on their first option than German players.
limits: Narrative synthesis, no pooled effect. Tension with ecological-dynamics accounts, which reject mental representation.
agent_relevance: Supports switching modes by typicality and time rather than a single fixed strategy.

source: Macrocognition: From Theory to Toolbox (Front Psychol 2016)
finding: A field-history account repeats the headline as '80 to 90% of firefighter decisions' and lists replications. Note the rounding up from the original 81% (127/156).
numbers: Claim: RPD accounted for 80 to 90% of fireground decisions. Replications named: military leaders (Schmitt and Klein 1999), firefighters (Keren et al. 2013), offshore oil platform managers (Skriver 1998). Lab tests: Klein et al. 1995; Johnson and Raab 2003. Claim that RPD 'could never have been discovered under laboratory conditions' because the experience takes 10 to 20 years.
limits: Advocate summary, secondary. The percentage drifts between sources (81% original; 80 to 90% later).
agent_relevance: Treat the quoted 80 to 90% as a repeated summary of one 156-point data set, not of three independent replications. Count independent replications separately in claims.jsonl.

source: Wikipedia: Recognition primed decision (three variants) and the clinical-reasoning review PMC6900348
finding: Three variants as usually listed. V1 simple match: situation typical, action known, 'if then'. V2 diagnose: situation unfamiliar, actions known, build the picture (feature matching, story building). V3 evaluate course of action: situation understood, mental simulation of the option until it fits. Wikipedia words V3 loosely (running simulations of new actions until one fits).
numbers: Sport and medical reviews use Klein's wording: level 1 simple match, level 2 diagnose the situation, level 3 mental simulation of the first option (Bossard 2022; Ashford 2021). The clinical reasoning review says only experienced physicians can use RPD, and variation 2 needs deductive hypothesis testing.
limits: Wikipedia flags itself as needing more citations. Wording of V3 differs between sources.
agent_relevance: V1 = keep first. V2 = reopen the situation reading. V3 = test the first candidate by simulation or by running a check. Map each to a state and a program rule.

source: Cohen, Freeman, Wolf (1996) Metarecognition in Time-Stressed Decision Making: Recognizing, Critiquing, and Correcting. Human Factors
finding: Extension of RPD with a critique layer. Adds metarecognition: decide whether it is worth thinking more, find evidence-conclusion links, critique the situation model for incompleteness, conflict and unreliability, then fetch more or revise assumptions. Abstract only was read (via Crossref).
numbers: Illustrated on naval tactical decision making (no sample numbers in the abstract).
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: A named formal precursor to our rule: verify the recognised answer, and spend extra thought only when a critique finds a gap.

source: Lipshitz, Klein, Orasanu, Salas (2001) Taking stock of naturalistic decision making. J Behav Decis Making 14:331-352
finding: Decade review of NDM. Lists RPD among five main contributions. Names two open problems: the quantity and rigour of empirical work, and confirming the validity of prescriptive models. Abstract only (via Crossref).
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Even proponents say the prescriptive claim (use RPD to decide better) is unconfirmed. Our scaffold use is a hypothesis to test.

source: Klein et al. (2010 print) Rapid Decision Making on the Fire Ground: The Original Study Plus a Postscript. J Cogn Eng Decis Mak
finding: Published edit of the unpublished 1985 study with a new commentary. The abstract matches the technical report I read: 26 FGCs (mean 23 years), 156 decision points, under 12% with simultaneous comparison, over 80% recognition. Abstract only (via Crossref).
numbers: 26 officers, 23 years, 156 points, <12%, >80%.
limits: Abstract only; full text behind a paywall.
agent_relevance: Cite the 2010 paper for the study and the 1985 report (opened) for the details.

source: Patterson, Fournier, Pierce, Winterbottom, Tripp (2009) System Dynamics Modeling of the Time Course of the RPD Model. J Cogn Eng Decis Mak 3(3):253-279
finding: First dynamic simulation of RPD. A system dynamics model, based on lab 'conjunction benefits and costs', predicts decision priming: a recognised typical situation primes a decision, and if later cues violate expectations the switch to 'diagnose' is slower.
numbers: Simulated 'diagnose' decision took about 8 s when the situation was unfamiliar from the start and about 16 s (100% commitment) when it first looked typical and then expectations were violated.
limits: Simulation only; no human data fitted in this report. Times are model outputs.
agent_relevance: Gives a testable prediction for an LLM: after a confident first answer, a contradicting fact should cost extra steps to overturn. That is anchoring; our G2 needs real output evidence to break it.

source: Gevarter (1991) MoCog1: A Computer Simulation of Recognition-Primed Human Decision Making. NASA TM-103868
finding: Early program for single-pass recognition-primed choice driven by affect and implicit goals, built for NASA human-computer cooperation. It reproduces earlier findings about how implicit theories orient goals. It does not model mental simulation or comparing options.
numbers: 22-page report; one program (MoCog1); a follow-up MoCog2 planned for multi-step thought.
limits: Affect-centred and not validated against the fireground data. A model of single-pass response only.
agent_relevance: Shows that the earliest code versions of RPD were just match-and-act. The simulate-and-modify loop came later in other models.

source: Kunde & Darken (2006) A Mental Simulation-Based Decision-Making Architecture Applied to Ground Combat
finding: Computational mental simulation for combat entities: machine-learned event predictors feed a decision tree for fire or hold-fire decisions in COMBAT XXI. Preliminary results look like human firing behaviour.
numbers: Three predictive models (target richness, obscuring terrain effects, losses); the look-ahead uses no more than three variables, following Klein 1999; the decision component is a decision tree.
limits: Preliminary results, one simulation scenario, human comparison not detailed.
agent_relevance: A concrete engineering template for the 'simulate the option' step: small learned predictors plus a coded decision rule. Fits our rule that code, not the model, decides.

source: Mueller & Thanasuan (2014) Crossword expertise as recognitional decision making: an artificial intelligence approach. Front Psychol
finding: Computational model of expert crossword solving as recognition by fast memory search. In the human data, experts relied on fluent retrieval, and error correction and backtracking mattered less than in classic AI solvers.
numbers: Experts finished the puzzle in 5.3 +/- 2.5 min with 77.2 of 78 answers correct; no novice finished in 25 min (23.9 +/- 9.4 answers complete, 23.1 correct).
limits: One puzzle, two groups; group sizes not seen in the text I read.
agent_relevance: A worked case where the first retrieved candidate is usually right for experts and effort goes into retrieval, not backtracking. Maps to strong model priors plus a cheap crossing check.

source: Community pharmacists' decision-making patterns in clinical prescription checking: a simulation-based study (2025)
finding: Qualitative think-aloud test coded against RPD. Pharmacists mostly pattern-matched and switched to analysis when something did not fit (atypical dose, risky combination, conflicting history). Cues and expectancies were consistent across people; the action chosen varied a lot.
numbers: 12 community pharmacists in England, 3 simulated prescriptions each, Zoom, deductive coding by RPD components (goals, cues, expectancies, actions). 7 of 12 had 1 to 3 years of experience.
limits: N=12, mostly junior; simulated task; it contrasts with an earlier study where pharmacists were mainly analytic.
agent_relevance: The switch trigger matches G1: analysis starts when an expectancy is violated, not on a timer.

source: Naikar (2010) A Comparison of the Decision Ladder Template and the Recognition-Primed Decision Model (DSTO-TR-2397)
finding: Compares RPD with the cognitive-work-analysis decision ladder on origins, concepts, knowledge elicitation, representation and design implications. Finds similarities and significant differences. Only the abstract and summary were read.
numbers: Five comparison factors; no data.
limits: Abstract-level reading. Conceptual comparison, no experiment.
agent_relevance: The decision ladder is the main formal rival in design work; its shortcut paths (observation straight to action) mirror keep-first.
